short: The name Nervii is associated with that part of Gaul, which is now northeastern France and Belgium, as, for example, Dux tractus Armoricani et Nervicani in Notitia. The name comes from the ancient Gallic tribe after which the area was named: the Nervii, but from Tacitus we learn that according to the version of the Nervii themselves, their tribe had Germanic roots. «The Treveri and Nervii claim a Germanic origin and, moreover, are proud of it, as if the boast of such affinity could save them from their similarity to the Gauls and the inherent weakness of those». During the period of the early empire a large number of auxiliary units were recruited from this area, some of which survived long enough to appear in Notitia, such as those listed in Dux Britanniarum. This area later became known as the Civitas Nerviorum; presumably Nervian units were recruited from this region. Auxilia (latin) - an auxiliary unit of the Roman army.  There is a strong opinion that auxilia units consisted of barbarians-volunteers (primarily Germanic). Vegetius directly mentions that the legions were composed of Roman citizens, and the auxilia of barbarians. About the internal organisation of the auxilia nothing is definitely known, but most likely, the structure of these units in the 4th century was no different from the legions. While the legions were composed of forcefully conscripted Romanised barbarians who lived on the territory of the Empire, in the auxilia served mainly volunteers from the Germanic tribes beyond the Rhine. Such system led to the fact that the auxiliaries became superior to the legionnaires in terms of their combat qualities.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
